name: Bank angle
seoDesc: Bank angle: work out speed (v) from the turn radius and the banking angle. A free physics calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: speed (v) is what the Bank angle calculator works out, and it gets there from the turn radius, the banking angle, the banking angle (θ) and the speed (v). It is built for a lab report, a problem set or a sanity check on a physical situation. The unit chips sit next to the boxes, which is where most hand-calculation mistakes start.

sections.title: How does the Bank angle calculator work?
sections.html:
The Bank angle calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports speed (v) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (what to calculate?, what to calculate? (2) and maximum or minimum speed?); then you type in the turn radius (r), the banking angle (θ), the banking angle (θ) (2) and the speed (v) (2).

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Bank angle calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Speed (v)=the square root of (-G × turn radius (r) × (friction coefficient (μ) × maximum or minimum speed? + the tangent of (banking angle (θ))) ÷ (friction coefficient (μ) × maximum or minimum speed? × the tangent of (banking angle (θ)) − 1))
Custom value of μ=(-G × turn radius (r) × the tangent of (banking angle (θ)) + (speed (v) ^ 2)) ÷ (maximum or minimum speed? × (G × turn radius (r) + (speed (v) ^ 2) × the tangent of (banking angle (θ))))
Speed (v)=the square root of (-G × turn radius (r) × (friction coefficient (μ) × maximum or minimum speed? + the tangent of (angle of banking (θ))) ÷ (friction coefficient (μ) × maximum or minimum speed? × the tangent of (angle of banking (θ)) − 1))
Custom value of μ=(-G × turn radius (r) × the tangent of (angle of banking (θ)) + (speed (v) ^ 2)) ÷ (maximum or minimum speed? × (G × turn radius (r) + (speed (v) ^ 2) × the tangent of (angle of banking (θ))))
True airspeed (v)=the square root of (G × radius of the turn (r) × the tangent of (angle of banking (θ)))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Suppose Where are we turning? set to On the ground, What to calculate? set to Radius, Maximum or minimum speed? set to Maximum and Friction coefficient (μ) set to Tire, dry asphalt. Working through the relationship above gives True airspeed (v) = 2.6183 m/s and Angle of banking (θ) = 10 deg.

Read it as a template. Every number above can be replaced with one of yours; only the relationship between them is fixed.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: True airspeed (v) = 2.6183 m/s and Angle of banking (θ) = 10 deg should be roughly the size you expected from Where are we turning? set to On the ground and What to calculate? set to Radius.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Bank angle calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Solving a problem set where the algebra is more interesting than the arithmetic
  • Writing up a lab result and needing a quick cross-check
  • Testing whether an answer is physically plausible before you trust it
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the turn radius, the banking angle and the banking angle (θ) — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Bank angle calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns speed (v), derived from the turn radius, the banking angle and the banking angle (θ). Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Bank angle calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the turn radius, the banking angle, the banking angle (θ) and the speed (v), which is 13 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter turn radius (r) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Turn radius (r) opens in meters and the chip beside it offers 34 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (5 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports True airspeed (v) = 2.6183 m/s. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Bank angle calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
